item.title: For women and children in West Africa, medical treatment often came too late. Then one model changed where care begins.
item.description:
The medicines already existed. The challenge was reaching people in time. Muso’s model of proactive community healthcare is showing what becomes possible when care moves closer to families.

In 2009, a community health worker in the bustling capital of Bamako, Mali, found a young boy at home who had become dangerously ill within a matter of hours. Recognizing he needed urgent medical care, she arranged for him to be taken to a health facility.

The journey was five kilometers, but distance was only part of the challenge. The boy’s father carried him on foot, then into an ambulance, then back on foot to cross a river, then into another ambulance.

“At that time, it was very difficult for the ambulance to move within the community, because there were no clear roads,” says Djoumé Diakité, MD, co-founder and Mali Country Director of Muso, a nonprofit that had launched its Rapid Care approach the year before to address poor health outcomes in the region.

At the clinic, a handful of doctors and nurses were responsible for everything from prenatal care to emergency medicine. The boy had severe malaria-related anemia and needed a blood transfusion. “It was very difficult to have access to blood at the facility,” Diakité says. “I gave my own blood [to replenish the supply].”

The boy spent 10 days in the clinic — a sacrifice his family could scarcely afford. Ten days at his bedside meant 10 days without work or wages for his father. Saving the boy’s life also meant feeding the parent caring for him.

“That story touched my heart deeply — I imagine myself in that [situation], choosing between feeding [my] family and bringing one of them to the [health clinic],” Diakité says.

He and the community health worker (CHW) who found the boy know exactly what would have happened had she not reached him when she did.

For decades, the global fight against child mortality focused on building hospitals, funding medical breakthroughs, and expanding formal health systems. Yet in places like Mali, one of the most powerful tools for saving children’s lives was hiding in plain sight: CHWs — mostly women — already living among the families they served, trusted by their neighbors but largely overlooked, underfunded, and excluded from the center of health policy.

Muso set out to change that.

The system’s blind spot

When Muso launched Rapid Care in 2008, about one in seven children in Mali died before their fifth birthday. The medicines to save many of them already existed; the problem was access. In Bamako’s poorest neighborhoods, five kilometers could feel like fifty. And even families who reached a clinic often faced another barrier: Since 1984, national law had required patients to contribute to the cost of their own care, giving community health associations the authority to charge fees at every step.

These impossible trade‑offs were playing out in communities across sub-Saharan Africa. Diakité and one of his Muso cofounders Ari Johnson, a physician and global health researcher, saw that healthcare was arriving too late. How could they remove the financial and logistical barriers to preventive and diagnostic services, and reach families before illness became an emergency?

For years, CHWs in countries like Mali and Côte d’Ivoire operated in a policy gap: essential in practice, but unsupported and unrecognized on paper. They delivered care without salaries, legal recognition, or the protections that come with formal workforce status. Globally, women make up about 67 percent of the health and social care workforce, yet they remain disproportionately concentrated in lower-paid and unpaid roles. Women in Global Health estimates that at least 6 million women worldwide work as unpaid or underpaid CHWs. (In Bambara, a lingua franca of Mali, Muso means “woman.”)

CHWs were already right there in Mali’s underserved communities, already familiar to neighbors. Diakité and Johnson advocated for governments to invest in them. Local authorities pushed back.

“They were not confident [that] people who never went to the school of medicine could provide quality care at the household level,” Diakité recalls. “The chief medical officer said to us, ‘If you make a mistake, I will send you to jail.’”

Slow access to care created a vicious cycle. Conditions that could have been treated early became emergencies, overwhelming clinics with preventable cases and stretching scarce resources ever thinner. “Once you lose that first contact and the trust is broken, the whole system [pays] the price,” explains Christian Rusangwa, Muso’s Director of Technical Assistance.

Muso’s leaders understood that empowering CHWs was worth the risk — that reducing child mortality in Mali, and now through Muso-supported programs in Côte d’Ivoire and Zambia, could begin with something as simple as a knock on the door.

The woman everyone calls

In Côte d’Ivoire’s rural Madinani district, that knock on the door often comes from Brigitte Kouadio, a professional CHW who is trained, paid, and supervised through a partnership between Muso and the Ministry of Health through proactive community case management, or ProCCM. On paper, she covers about 107 households; in reality, she is woven into daily life. Kouadio visits homes, listens for symptoms, and decides who she can treat herself and who needs to go to a facility.

One recent afternoon, a young boy named Okore stopped playing and went to bed with a fever. His mother, Diahou Apo Natacha, called Kouadio, who immediately came to the house to examine Okore and perform a rapid malaria test. When the test came back negative and the boy’s condition looked serious, she gave basic care, then arranged transport to the hospital.

“By the grace of God, Muso covered all the costs — we did not pay anything,” Natacha recalls. After three days and a blood transfusion, they returned home. Kouadio visited again to go over the medication and show the family how to give it correctly. Natacha says the CHWs in her village “take very good care of us;” Kouadio says that since that episode, the family has fully embraced her, and they have “become like a second family.”

At first, families didn’t believe that care could really be free, assuming there must be a catch. Only after they saw, again and again, that they truly did not have to pay — whether at home or at the hospital — did they start calling as soon as something was wrong. For families used to losing days in the search of healthcare, Diakite says, it was “like they discovered gold in front of their door.”

Rebuilding the system around community health workers

Behind Natacha’s phone call, there’s now an entire architecture. Since 2008, Muso and the Malian government have worked to co‑develop a model that treats CHWs as the organizing principle; in late 2019, Côte d’Ivoire’s Ministry of Health partnered with Muso to adopt that model into its national health system. Health workers are recruited from within their communities; Muso and government partners train them, equip them with protocols and tools, and pay them a salary. Supervisors visit regularly to review cases, and clinics are staffed and stocked to receive referrals. Care is free at home and in facilities.

By rebuilding trust and bringing care closer to home, the model not only reduces preventable illness and death — it helps stabilize the health system itself, allowing every level of care to function more effectively.

A common thread supporting the initiative’s success: Trust the people closest to the challenges to develop the most effective solutions. This principle extends all the way to the apps and platforms CHWs use to manage cases. “The state-of-the-art digital tools are designed not in Silicon Valley, [but] in Yirimadio, in the Mopti region, in Madinani or Adzopé,” Johnson says. “They’re designed with the CHWs who understand the problems and the best ways to solve them. That’s the key.”

From village fix to national backbone

Muso is now working with Côte d’Ivoire’s Ministry of Health on a legal framework that would give CHWs formal status, stipends, training, and social protection. The government counts about 12,000 CHWs nationwide; over the course of just 15 months, Muso helped extend free care, supportive supervision, and digital tools to 8,000 of them. Through a program known as CMU+, the Ivorian government rolled out free care across 2,823 rural health facilities from May to December 2025, opening access to 13 million eligible people.

Zambia is next. In 2024, the country’s Ministry of Health signed a memorandum of understanding with Muso to adapt the model in a politically stable nation where healthcare is already free nationwide. For Rusangwa, success there would demonstrate that centering CHWs can improve outcomes not only in places grappling with conflict and fragile health systems, but also in stable, peaceful countries — a crucial step toward Muso’s ultimate goal: “to end the child and maternal mortality crises and deliver universal health coverage at scale.”

In Diapé, that ambition looks like a mother reaching for her phone when her child grows hot with fever, and a CHW in a khaki Muso vest walking toward a house where she is welcomed like family. For families on the margins of care, the future does not arrive with a ribbon‑cutting; it knocks on the door.

item.title: Reflections and Highlights from the 2026 Skoll World Forum
item.description:
The 2026 Skoll World Forum took place April 21–24 in Oxford, U.K. and online, bringing together 1,500 social entrepreneurs, philanthropists, storytellers, government officials, and private-sector leaders to explore sustainable solutions to the complex challenges we face.

Inspired by the cycles of regeneration seen in ecosystems across our planet, this year’s Forum centered around “The Ecology of Us,” highlighting the inherent connections and parallels between humans and the rest of the natural world. At a time when global crises loom large, the gathering reminded us of our innate capacity to build a more peaceful, prosperous future—together.

Over four days of plenaries, panels, workshops, dinners, and serendipitous encounters along Oxford’s historic streets, the Skoll community came together to test the boundaries of what’s possible, from strengthening health systems by investing in two-way trust-building to cultivating forest-positive economies in the Amazon. In exploring what it means for people and planet to thrive, we learned how to transform siloes into more cohesive ecosystems grounded in care, compassion, and resilience.

Alongside conversations with global thought leaders, such as Nobel Peace Prize Laureate Juan Manuel Santos and Noubar Afeyan (Aurora Humanitarian Initiative; Flagship Pioneering), delegates found space to nourish themselves for the work ahead via meditation, intentional movement, and more.

The week kicked off with an inspiring—and deeply funny—conversation between comedian and philanthropist Trevor Noah and Wawira Njiru (Food4Education). They explored Wawira’s journey as a social entrepreneur, how to set and achieve progressively bolder goals, building community ownership over solutions, and preserving the dignity of those the solutions are meant to serve. It was a pragmatic yet optimistic conversation that set the tone for what was to come.

The celebration continued with the Skoll Awards Ceremony, where the Foundation welcomed the newest recipients of the Skoll Award for Social Innovation into our community. Grace Matlhape of SmartStart, Tarun Cherukuri of Indus Action, and Ahson Rabbani of ChildLife Foundation shared moving accounts of the forces that have shaped their lives and that motivate them to keep pushing for lasting impact.

Watch the Foundation’s closing film to see highlights from throughout the week:

Several prominent conversations at the Forum centered on artificial intelligence. Attendees discussed safety, access, and how nations across the global majority are poised to assert transformative influence over a deeply disruptive technology.

Throughout the week, a recurring insight emerged: the social sector’s most pressing constraint is not the availability of resources or expertise, but the design of the systems through which those assets flow. Speakers such as Angela Gichaga (enAble Advisors) and Kate Kallot (Amini) challenged delegates to rethink not just how much capital is available or what technologies like AI can do, but what the systems that control those resources look like, and who gets to build that infrastructure.

Then, in a stirring plenary talk on Friday, Alessandra Orofino (Peri Productions) made the case that culture is not simply a backdrop to our work, but one of the most powerful levers for creating lasting change. The message was apt: music, art, and film were ubiquitous throughout the week. Ricky Kej led an ensemble through a high-energy performance, actor and humanitarian Richard Gere and Kynan Tegar and Lucía Ixchiu (If Not Us Then Who?) screened two new films, and delegates were on their feet for spirited singalongs with Astrid Jorgensen’s Pub Choir and, in a delightful surprise, a guitar-slinging Francis Collins (formerly of the National Institutes of Health).

The week culminated with a performance by artist and social activist Madame Gandhi, whose music incorporates soundscapes from the frontlines of climate change, like the otherworldly sound of crackling ice as ancient glaciers melt into the sea.

To revisit conversations or listen in for the first time, explore our content archive, which contains recordings of all plenaries and performances as well as a selection of sessions and panels.

item.title: Skoll Foundation Announces Winners of the 2026 Skoll Award for Social Innovation
item.description:
With innovative solutions to some of the world’s most urgent challenges, three social entrepreneurs are building a better future for all

Today, the Skoll Foundation announced the three organizations that will receive the 2026 Skoll Award for Social Innovation: ChildLife Foundation, SmartStart, and Indus Action. The $2 million award provides unrestricted support to nonprofit organizations with a proven track record of advancing transformational social change on intractable global issues.

Through innovative public-private partnerships, thoughtful community integration, and systems-level thinking, the 2026 Awardees are driving measurable progress on child health in Pakistan, early learning and development in South Africa, and civic technology and public benefits access in India. Together, these remarkable organizations are advancing a sustainable world of peace and prosperity for all.

The Foundation will present the Awards and celebrate the leaders of each recipient organization during the 23rd annual Skoll World Forum, held April 21–24 in Oxford, U.K. and online. The Awards Ceremony will take place Thursday, April 23, from 5–6:30pm BST at the New Theatre in Oxford and via livestream. Click here to register to attend the Forum online.

“This year’s winners of the Skoll Award for Social Innovation prove that when bold, creative leaders set their sights on a problem, their resolve and commitment lead to global systems change. Through innovative partnerships with affected communities and cross-sector collaboration, they are driving impact and lasting change in the fields of health, education, and public benefits,” said Marla Blow, CEO & President of the Skoll Foundation. “Even in the face of profound shocks to the social impact space, these organizations are not simply maintaining their impact; they are increasing it exponentially. We hope their stories will inspire other social entrepreneurs to continue their pursuit of transformational change.”

More details about the 2026 Awardees:

ChildLife Foundation

Pakistan faces one of the highest child mortality rates in the world, with nearly 1,000 children dying every day from treatable conditions like pneumonia. ChildLife Foundation works to prevent those deaths by strengthening Pakistan’s struggling pediatric emergency care system. It partners with government to rehabilitate and manage pediatric ERs within public hospitals, delivering world-class care through modern facilities and equipment, efficient systems, and well-trained teams. Additionally, ChildLife Foundation’s 24/7 telemedicine network links over 300 district hospitals to pediatric specialists, covering 90 percent of the population. This system has achieved a tenfold reduction in child mortality in the ERs ChildLife manages. By building government doctors’ capacity and scaling to 40 modernized ERs and more than 400 telemedicine sites, the organization hopes to deliver life-saving care to 20 million children each year.

SmartStart

High-quality early childhood care and education boosts child outcomes, creates new jobs, and enables parents to work. Yet in South Africa, over one million 3- to 5-year-olds don’t have access, perpetuating the economic exclusion of poor communities. SmartStart’s model enables underemployed community members to convert their homes and community spaces into licensed early learning enterprises for excluded children. By combining training, materials, coaching, compliance support and peer networks, SmartStart’s social franchise model makes quality early learning affordable, accessible and community-owned. At the same time, the model unlocks stable, dignified livelihood opportunities for thousands of microentrepreneurs. Through deep collaboration with government and other partners, SmartStart has grown into South Africa’s leading early learning network, with 15,000 programs currently reaching 160,000 children per week. The organization is now building the systems, capabilities and partnerships to grow its impact beyond its direct delivery footprint and reach 1 million children by 2030.

Indus Action

India spends $150 billion annually on more than 5,000 social protection programs, yet complex processes prevent nearly 800 million citizens from accessing the benefits they are entitled to receive. An estimated 25 percent of legislated benefits—including those for students, workers, and new mothers—never reach their intended recipients, trapping millions in cycles of poverty.  Indus Action bridges this gap through a three-pronged approach: building government delivery capacity; leveraging technology to design open-source, citizen-centric solutions; and using research to improve benefit-delivery systems. By engaging both citizens and state agencies, Indus Action is transforming constitutional commitments into impact by ensuring vulnerable Indians can access education, health care, and financial programs that provide pathways out of poverty. By 2030, the organization aims to seamlessly connect 30 million citizens to all the benefits for which they are eligible.

item.title: Skoll Foundation Welcomes Salah Goss As Chief Program Officer
item.description:
The Skoll Foundation and its Board of Directors are delighted to announce that Salah Goss has joined the Foundation as Chief Program Officer. Salah will play a pivotal role in the Foundation’s next chapter, overseeing our work to support social entrepreneurs and other innovators through strategic grantmaking and investing, storytelling, partnerships, and convenings—including the Skoll World Forum.

Salah brings more than 20 years of experience in the philanthropic, private, and public sectors and is an experienced champion of social entrepreneurs as powerful agents of change. She has spent her career building the systems, tools, and institutions that expand economic access for underserved communities across Africa, Latin America, Southeast Asia, the Caribbean, and the United States. She also founded Impulse 52, an advisory firm focused on fintech consulting services, strategic philanthropy, and corporate social impact.

“We are thrilled to welcome Salah to lead the design and execution of the Foundation’s programmatic strategy,” said Marla Blow, CEO and President of the Skoll Foundation. “Salah is an ambitious, visionary thinker who has long been committed to driving systems change, and her track record in financial inclusion will enable us to deepen our work to expand economic opportunity around the world. Her experience collaborating across sectors and geographies and her deep relationships with the communities she’s served make her an extraordinary addition to the team.”

“The Skoll Foundation is a global champion of the kind of bold, community-centered work that I believe in,” Salah said. “It is a privilege to serve this community of social entrepreneurs and other change leaders around the world, and I look forward to supporting them with the resources and connections they need in order to tackle the most urgent challenges of our time.”

Salah spent more than a decade at Mastercard, where she helped establish its financial inclusion line of business—work that required building new technologies and earned her a patent. She went on to lead the Mastercard Lab for Financial Inclusion in Kenya, which was recognized as a top five fintech lab by Fintech Magazine for its use of human-centered innovation and design. As Senior Vice President, Salah oversaw Mastercard’s philanthropic giving across the United States, Canada, Latin America, and the Caribbean, where she established a robust, commercially sustainable social-impact portfolio, unlocking capital to support over 1 million small businesses.

Earlier in her career, Salah oversaw the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation’s financial inclusion work in Nigeria, Indonesia, and the Philippines, where her team helped pioneer mobile money as a financial inclusion tool. She began her career in Africa, first in Senegal as Grants Officer for the George Soros Open Society Initiative for West Africa, and later in Egypt with a focus on Islamic banking. Salah is a World Economic Forum and Schwab Foundation Social Entrepreneur awardee, an Aspen Institute Finance Leader Fellow, a Rockefeller Foundation Bellagio Center 2024 Resident, and a Cornell University Thoreau Fellow.

Please join us in welcoming Salah to the Foundation. We are excited to see how she deploys her experience, perspective, and passion to harness the power of social entrepreneurship toward transformative and lasting social change.

item.title: Widening the Frame: Indigenous Land Rights and the Future of Climate Policy
item.description:
A growing movement shows that protecting the world’s forests—and the people who have safeguarded them for centuries—is one of the most powerful, and overlooked, tools in the fight against climate change.

By Lee Helland & Carina Mia Wong

A woman stands at the edge of the Amazon Rainforest. Behind her, an explosion of life—thousands of animal species, billions of trees, lush canopy. Ahead, another kind: Humanity.

People from every corner of the Earth fill the city of Belém, Brazil. It’s a sea of color, music, and emotion as they dance and stomp across asphalt, past highrises in the hot, humid air. A paper snake the length of a city block ripples overhead.

The woman wipes sweat from her temples. Her purple baseball cap is soaked through, its message blunt:

DERECHOS A LA TIERRA ¡YA!

Land rights—now.

The woman is Joan Carling, a human rights activist and the executive director of Indigenous Peoples Rights International (IPRI). The scene unfolded at COP30, the climate summit hosted by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) in November 2025. A member of the Kankanaey people of the Philippines, Carling was one of at least 5,000 Indigenous representatives in attendance, a more than tenfold increase over recent COPs.

Their message to international climate-action decision makers is simple: Indigenous Peoples have the right to own and manage their ancestral land, and honoring those rights is a crucial lever in climate action.

In much of the Western world, even well-informed news consumers may find this message unfamiliar, set against the dominant climate script—electrify everything, build green tech, cut emissions. But COP30 made one thing clear: That conversation is beginning to widen.

“Those in power are using their might to further marginalize us instead of recognizing the role that we do in protecting our environment,” Carling says.

While Indigenous leaders welcomed greater openness at COP30, barriers remained. One Big Think producer logged more than eight miles a day walking the convention center. One in every 25 participants represented the fossil fuel industry, according to Kick Big Polluters Out.

item.title: Transformation and Renewal in the Impact Ecosystem: Our 2026 Annual Letter
item.description:
Ecologists tell us that the true strength of a forest lies not in the trees’ towering trunks or the grandeur of their awe-inspiring canopy. Rather, the source of its resilience is largely invisible, coursing beneath the surface within the mycelium—delicate fungal threads that facilitate resource-sharing and communication. By channeling energy and resources upward, these connections enable forests to regrow and renew, ensuring collective survival.

As I reflect on 2025 and the year ahead, this regenerative system seems an apt metaphor for the social impact sector. The dismantling of USAID and other multilateral financing created seismic shocks for nonprofits worldwide. Organizations confronted sudden, profound disruptions that ripped through the ecosystem. Many in our sector are still feeling the aftershocks.

But that’s not how this story ends.

The remarkable social entrepreneurs in the Skoll Foundation community absorbed the initial shock, reacting swiftly to stabilize their work and address immediate needs. Now, they have moved into a strategic response phase. Just as the mycelium enables forests to rise again, our partners are drawing on the strength of their connections as they navigate this time of change.

I am heartened to see this movement toward collective recovery as change leaders graduate into the next phase of intentional experimentation and thoughtful evolution. Witnessing this community regroup and reshape their work has been inspiring.

In 2026, the Foundation, too, is evolving. We’re embracing strategic recalibration, anchored in our longstanding commitment to championing our partners. Reflecting on the last five years at the Foundation with eight months as CEO, I’m feeling both hopeful about the opportunities that lie ahead and wiser about what it will take to get there. As the Foundation prepares to gather in Oxford and online for the Skoll World Forum in April, I want to share why we remain optimistic about finding opportunity amid crisis—and how we get there, together.

A Year of Recalibration

Over the past several months, I have met with changemakers, peer funders, private-sector leaders, and government officials around the world, from Rwanda to New York. The message I heard has been remarkably consistent: Leaders are fortifying themselves for a new era of social impact. They’re ready to be bold and ambitious in reshaping the global impact ecosystem to function more effectively and sustainably.

The Foundation has been exploring our role in that transformation, even as our fundamental purpose of supporting our partners remains constant. If the last year has taught us anything, it’s that philanthropy has both an opportunity and a responsibility to rethink our approach to catalyzing change, including how we resource locally led innovations and build connective tissue to ensure the global funding system is more resilient and coordinated. It means collaborating across sectors and geographies in new ways, helping our partners harness technology to turbocharge their work, and redefining business models to prioritize greater partnership and proximity.

I recognize that philanthropy cannot replace the sovereign support that previously underpinned the global development arena. At the same time, philanthropy can capitalize some of the critical rebuilding work that must be done. It’s also essential to uncover new sources of capital. In the years ahead, I’m optimistic that deeper collaboration across the private, philanthropic, and public sectors will finally unlock the kind of blended capital partnerships many of us have long envisioned.

There are other levers we can pull in addition to funding. We are exploring new opportunities to leverage our global platform to support our community, such as our partnerships last year to convene changemakers in Nairobi and São Paulo, or championing proximate storytelling around the world through the Solutions Storytelling Project.

Here’s more of what the next chapter looks like for us at the Foundation:

Investing in, connecting, and championing social entrepreneurs remains our North Star.

Through every shift and shock, we continue to believe social entrepreneurs hold the key to tackling humanity’s most pressing problems. This commitment has not wavered since Jeff established the Foundation in 1999 with social entrepreneurship as his driving force.

In 2025, nearly 80 percent of Foundation funding supported social entrepreneurship, with 55 percent directly reaching Skoll Awardees and other social entrepreneurs; we expect that level of support to continue. Strengthening trust and seeding connections both with and among our community remain critical to ensuring our decisions are responsive to emerging needs and informed by lived experience.

Over the past 12 months, our partners’ agility and resolve have been on full display as they responded to shifts in the funding environment. Across our portfolio, partners reported $305 million in global funding lost and another $74 million in lost domestic funding.

In response, the Foundation sought to help our community weather immediate crises as well as support their efforts to adapt for the long term. We launched the Pivot Fund and disbursed a total of $28.1 million via emergency grants and “pivot” funding to support partners to explore strategic adaptations to their operating models.

We’ve noted several themes in those pivots. Partners are experimenting with new revenue models, such as fee-for-service offerings. Many are reorienting to emphasize local leadership by equipping national governments to be the “payer” and “doer,” delegating authority to regional offices, or engaging community-based partners. Another major trend is the continued embrace of technology-driven solutions. Many organizations are developing data platforms, digital tools, or AI-powered services to increase efficiency, expand reach, or create new revenue streams.

Nonprofits are also strengthening their work through mergers and acquisitions. One example is the strategic merger of the International Foundation for Valuing Impacts (IFVI) and Capitals Coalition. The groups had already identified strong alignment in their work to advance impact evaluation in the social sector. Funding constraints in early 2025 served as the impetus to deepen those talks.

The Skoll Foundation accelerated the remaining balance of our grant to IFVI to help facilitate the transaction. Now, leadership is confident the new entity can sustain its impact over the long term: “Not a day goes by that I don’t think this was absolutely the right decision,” Capitals Coalition Executive Director and former IFVI CEO Rob Zochowski shared.

Together, these shifts reflect a community that is not retreating—but transforming. Partners are building more resilient, locally grounded, and financially diverse models that can withstand future disruptions.

To best fulfill our commitment to our partners, we have zeroed in on three core funding priorities.

As we’ve shared previously, the Foundation has reaffirmed our work in three areas, each of which stems from our longstanding commitments, experience, and investments:

  1. Preventing deforestation by supporting land tenure for Indigenous Peoples and local communities
  2. Strengthening global health systems through community health workers
  3. Expanding economic opportunity by supporting smallholder agriculture and girls’ education

 

These areas are distinct yet mutually reinforcing. Accessible schools, well-equipped community health workers, productive family farms, clean and safe ecosystems—these are the tentpoles that hold up a community and enable the people who live there to thrive.

We know that lasting change comes from within, and that the richest solutions and insights come from communities themselves. As such, we aim to channel our resources to those most proximate to the challenges at hand.

For example, since 2022, we have supported Africa Frontline First (AFF), a collaborative, cross-sector initiative to scale community health worker (CHW) programs across more than 15 African countries. To date, the fund has unlocked $240 million in private and public investments in CHW programs across the continent. We recently announced an additional $6 million investment in the next phase of this work, the AFF Sustainability and Resilience Fund, to accelerate countries’ paths to domestically financed, self-reliant, and nationally scaled CHW programs.

In climate, the evidence is clear: when Indigenous Peoples and local communities have secure land rights—combined with meaningful decision-making power over their natural resources—deforestation rates drop significantly. In recognition of this essential role in stewarding climate-critical ecosystems, the Skoll Foundation joined 34 governments and philanthropies in pledging a collective $1.8 billion to help secure and enforce these land rights.

We are experimenting with different forms of catalytic capital.

About $1.1 trillion sits in the endowments of private US-based foundations, representing a vitally important opportunity to put our capital to work toward impact. Leveraging our entire balance sheet to drive systems change—in partnership with our investment manager, Capricorn Investment Group—has been a cornerstone of my approach since I joined the Foundation in 2021. I consider it a priority to uncover new and innovative program-related investments that enable our sector to meet this moment.

Today, about 80 percent of our endowment aligns with impact objectives across four interconnected priority areas: climate change mitigation and resilience, economic opportunity, health care, and responsible stewardship. This does not require economic concessions: our financial returns continue to meet or exceed the performance of comparable asset classes.

We are excited that, in 2024 (the most recent year for which we have data), Skoll made 54 investments in mission-aligned funds or impact-oriented companies. Through our partners, we supported 141 companies or platforms advancing climate change solutions and invested in 33 companies focused on financial inclusion, five employee-owned businesses, and 50 companies focused on education.

Our support for Apis & Heritage Capital Partners, one of the 2025 Skoll Award for Social Innovation recipients, illustrates our close partnership with Capricorn. A&H is an investment fund that increases economic stability in the United States by transitioning small and medium-size businesses to employee ownership. We activated our endowment to make the Award investment in A&H—a first for the Foundation. The fact that this Award was structured as a commercial investment through Capricorn demonstrates our expectation of reaching our endowment’s market-return threshold.

We are evolving our operations to more meaningfully convene our community.

The sector has expressed a deep desire for connection. The Foundation is leaning further into our role as a convener, including exploring opportunities to gather changemakers in innovation hubs around the world, such as East Africa. We’re also looking to gather in spaces where capital, innovation, and influence intersect. Washington, DC is one such crossroads.

As we’ve shared previously, we are moving our headquarters to DC, where we look forward to engaging more seamlessly with crucial allies in the public and private sectors to scale what works, as well as to connecting our partners to the conversations shaping global change. The sector has long understood that collaboration results in better outcomes, but the imperative to work together now feels mission critical. And with governments and institutions similarly in flux, we believe this move will position us to identify newly opened windows of opportunity for more effective collaborations.

This transition to DC is underway, and we are seeing encouraging momentum: new partnerships, a compelling talent pool, and greater geographic proximity to many of our existing partners. I also acknowledge this transition has been challenging, as we are saying farewell to some members of our staff. These individuals have our full support to make the choices that are right for them and their families, and we invite you to join us in celebrating their enduring contributions to building an organization that I am proud to steward into its next chapter.

The Power of Resiliency

Most days, I walk along a wooded path near my home. I note how the trees change character from season to season, how the air hangs differently. Change is everywhere, but one thing remains the same: the reliable cycles of regeneration.

For us at the Foundation, our constant is our vision: to build a sustainable world of peace and prosperity for all. Nature reminds us that how we get there might shift alongside the conditions of our environment. As we do so, we can draw strength from connections with those who share our ecosystem—just as forests have done for millennia.

One enduring characteristic of social entrepreneurs is their resilience: I have seen them fall in love with a problem and commit to solving it, even as the context and support structures change. Their spirit is a powerful reminder that out of crisis, we can rise to the challenge.

We look forward to gathering our community for the Skoll World Forum, April 21–24, when we will celebrate our newest class of Skoll Awardees—a group of leaders who acutely understand what it takes to push through difficulties to create change. It is our deepest honor to serve our community and the broader social impact space by amplifying their remarkable stories.

With gratitude and grit,
Marla Blow, CEO

The post Transformation and Renewal in the Impact Ecosystem: Our 2026 Annual Letter appeared first on Skoll.org.

We activated our endowment to make the Award investment in A&H—a first for the Foundation. The fact that this Award was structured as a commercial investment through Capricorn demonstrates our expectation of reaching our endowment’s market-return threshold.

We are evolving our operations to more meaningfully convene our community.

The sector has expressed a deep desire for connection. The Foundation is leaning further into our role as a convener, including exploring opportunities to gather changemakers in innovation hubs around the world, such as East Africa. We’re also looking to gather in spaces where capital, innovation, and influence intersect. Washington, DC is one such crossroads.

As we’ve shared previously, we are moving our headquarters to DC, where we look forward to engaging more seamlessly with crucial allies in the public and private sectors to scale what works, as well as to connecting our partners to the conversations shaping global change. The sector has long understood that collaboration results in better outcomes, but the imperative to work together now feels mission critical. And with governments and institutions similarly in flux, we believe this move will position us to identify newly opened windows of opportunity for more effective collaborations.

This transition to DC is underway, and we are seeing encouraging momentum: new partnerships, a compelling talent pool, and greater geographic proximity to many of our existing partners. I also acknowledge this transition has been challenging, as we are saying farewell to some members of our staff. These individuals have our full support to make the choices that are right for them and their families, and we invite you to join us in celebrating their enduring contributions to building an organization that I am proud to steward into its next chapter.

The Power of Resiliency

Most days, I walk along a wooded path near my home. I note how the trees change character from season to season, how the air hangs differently. Change is everywhere, but one thing remains the same: the reliable cycles of regeneration.

For us at the Foundation, our constant is our vision: to build a sustainable world of peace and prosperity for all. Nature reminds us that how we get there might shift alongside the conditions of our environment. As we do so, we can draw strength from connections with those who share our ecosystem—just as forests have done for millennia.

One enduring characteristic of social entrepreneurs is their resilience: I have seen them fall in love with a problem and commit to solving it, even as the context and support structures change. Their spirit is a powerful reminder that out of crisis, we can rise to the challenge.

We look forward to gathering our community for the Skoll World Forum, April 21–24, when we will celebrate our newest class of Skoll Awardees—a group of leaders who acutely understand what it takes to push through difficulties to create change. It is our deepest honor to serve our community and the broader social impact space by amplifying their remarkable stories.

With gratitude and grit,
Marla Blow, CEO

item.title: Asian Stories, Asian Filmmakers: Season Three of Solutions Inside Out is Here
item.description:
Launched in 2023, the Solutions Storytelling Project, a collaboration between the Video Consortium and the Skoll Foundation, connects regional filmmakers and social entrepreneurs to share stories of change with global audiences. The result is Solutions Inside Out, a series of vibrant short documentaries about—and by—local voices catalyzing social change within their communities.

In its third season, Solutions Inside Out features 16 inspirational short films highlighting stories of change from India, Thailand, the Philippines, Indonesia, Nepal, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. The series continues to uplift the narratives of proximate changemakers as told by proximate storytellers, all while transcending borders to share universal messages of resilience and hope.

Watch the trailer for Season Three below and subscribe to our YouTube channel to join us for each film’s world premiere, featuring live conversations with the filmmakers, stars of the films, and leaders from the featured organizations.

As films are released throughout the coming weeks, we’ll add them to the playlist below. Want to catch up on previous seasons? View Season One and Season Two online.
